analysis.one_liner: Creates a voluntary Medicare prescription drug benefit, subsidizing premiums for lower-income seniors, funded by higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.headline: The Medicare drug coverage bill drew a Republican sponsor, a Democratic cosponsor, and only one committee referral — the Senate Finance Committee never acted, and it died without a vote when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SPICE Act would have created a voluntary prescription drug benefit for everyone on Medicare, run through a new federal board. Seniors could buy drug coverage through a Medicare supplemental policy, a Medicare+Choice plan, or an employer plan, with the government paying the full premium for people under 150% of the poverty line and at least 25% for everyone else. The program would be paid for by large increases in federal tobacco taxes — nearly quadrupling the cigarette tax — plus general budget surplus money, and if the fund ran short the subsidies would automatically shrink.
analysis.who_benefits: People on Medicare, who in 1999 generally lacked prescription drug coverage. The bill would guarantee every Medicare beneficiary access to a drug plan with no pre-existing condition exclusions, subsidize the premium in full for those under 150% of the poverty line and at least 25% for everyone else, and require an appeals process so beneficiaries could get drugs left off a plan's formulary [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees every Medicare beneficiary access to outpatient prescription drug coverage with no pre-existing condition exclusions, through a supplemental policy, a Medicare+Choice plan, or a group health plan
Pays 100% of the premium cost for beneficiaries under 150% of the poverty line, a sliding percentage for those between 150% and 175%, and at least 25% for all other enrollees

Requires an appeals process so a beneficiary can obtain a medically necessary drug left off a plan's formulary, with at least the protections Medicare+Choice plans must provide, and 60 days' notice before formulary changes
Blocks insurers from cherry-picking healthier customers: the board may disapprove or revoke approval of any policy whose issuer is 'purposefully engaged' in favorable selection of beneficiaries

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco buyers and manufacturers, through sharply higher federal excise taxes — cigarettes would rise from $12 to $44.50 per thousand in 2000 and $47 thereafter, with similar increases on cigars, smokeless tobacco, and roll-your-own tobacco — plus appropriations from the federal on-budget surplus to cover any shortfall [S3].

drawbacks.text: The funding comes from steep tobacco excise tax increases, a tax that falls on smokers — disproportionately lower-income people — rather than on general progressive revenue

Subsidy payments go directly to private insurers, and both insurers and Medicare+Choice plans are free to decline to offer the coverage at all, so the benefit's availability depends on private companies choosing to participate

If the trust fund runs short, the board must first cut the standard subsidy as low as 10%, then tighten income thresholds, and can suspend assistance entirely — so the benefit is not guaranteed against future funding gaps
Beneficiaries who delay enrolling face a late-enrollment penalty that permanently reduces their subsidy, similar to the Medicare Part B penalty

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors without drug coverage, the benefit is substantial: near-universal access to a plan, full premium subsidies for the poorest beneficiaries, and protections against pre-existing-condition exclusions and formulary gaming. The costs are real, though. The tax base is regressive, the money flows through private insurers that cannot be compelled to participate, and the financing has a built-in escape valve that lets benefits erode instead of obligating Congress to appropriate more. It is a genuine attempt to solve a widely felt problem, but a structurally fragile one that a critic could fairly call both expensive for smokers and undercommitted by general revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Olympia Snowe introduced the SPICE Act on August 4, 1999, with Sen. Ron Wyden as a cosponsor, and spoke on the Senate floor about it that day and again in late September
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where no markup, hearing, or vote was ever scheduled
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, with the bill still sitting in committee, so no chamber ever voted on it

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private insurers kept the status quo — no new drug-benefit obligations but no subsidized drug program running through them either — and tobacco companies avoided a roughly fourfold cigarette tax increase. Medicare beneficiaries gained nothing; seniors went without a federal drug benefit for the rest of the 106th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and tobacco makers, not seniors

for.name: Sen. Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor in August and September 1999

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Senate Finance Committee (chaired by William Roth, R-DE)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral but never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote; no action followed the August 4, 1999 referral for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed the large federal tobacco tax increases the bill relied on for funding, as the industry consistently did on cigarette tax proposals of this era

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split appears in the record; support never grew beyond the Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor out of two total.

industries.industry: Private health insurers (Medigap and Medicare+Choice plans)
industries.note: Every dollar of federal assistance would be paid directly to the private issuer of a SPICE supplemental policy, Medicare+Choice plan, or group health plan, and only board-approved policies could sell the drug-only Medigap package — making private insurers the permanent channel for the benefit while giving them a new subsidized customer base.

The bill's funding mechanism raises the federal cigarette excise tax from $12 to $44.50 per thousand in 2000 and $47 from 2002, with parallel increases on cigars, snuff, chewing and pipe tobacco, cigarette papers and tubes, and a new tax on roll-your-own tobacco, plus floor-stock taxes and limits on re-importing previously exported products.

Extending drug coverage to millions of Medicare beneficiaries would greatly expand the insured market for prescriptions; the bill allows formularies and 'reasonable cost containment' but imposes no drug price controls.
